QC::Qubits.b: A two-level quantum system, the abstract equivalent of a classical bit. Its state is a unit vector \(|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\) with \(|\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1\).

QC::Qubits.f: Why does a qubit hold more information than a bit?
QC::Qubits.b: A bit is 0 or 1; a qubit is a superposition, and it can be in any of infinitely many states. That is not more classical information, though: measurement still returns only one bit, and the gain shows up only in interference and entanglement.

QC::Qubits.f: How many classical bits does n qubits represent?
QC::Qubits.b: Exactly \(2^n\). So 10 qubits = 1024 amplitudes, 20 qubits = about a million, 50 qubits exceeds the memory of a supercomputer. The state is exponential even though a single measurement is not.

QC::Qubits.f: What does measuring a qubit give?
QC::Qubits.b: 0 or 1, with probabilities \(|\alpha|^2\) and \(|\beta|^2\). After measurement the state is \(|0\rangle\) or \(|1\rangle\) respectively: one bit, and the phase is gone.

Every pure qubit state maps to a point on the unit sphere, with amplitudes \[ \alpha = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}, \qquad \beta = e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac{\theta}{2} \]
Two angles, so the state has two real parameters, as it should. The sphere is not a 3D physical space: distance on it is meaningless.

QC::Qubits.f: Where are the computational basis states on the Bloch sphere?
QC::Qubits.b: \(|0\rangle\) is the north pole and \(|1\rangle\) the south pole; the equator is the whole equator. Measuring along axis \(\hat n\) returns 0 or 1 with probability \((1 \pm \hat r\cdot\hat n)/2\).

QC::Qubits.f: What is the X gate, and what does it do?
QC::Qubits.b: Not \(X\)-rotation (that is \(R_x\)). The Pauli \(X\) is the NOT gate: it flips \(|0\rangle \leftrightarrow |1\rangle\), is its own inverse, and is the bit-flip. It swaps the Bloch sphere's \(\pm z\) and \(\pm x\) axes.

The phase flip: \(|0\rangle \to |0\rangle\), \(|1\rangle \to -|1\rangle\). It leaves populations untouched, so it is invisible in computational-basis measurement, but it shifts phase and therefore interferes.

The Hadamard: \(H = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\). It is its own inverse and rotates \(\pi\) about the axis between \(x\) and \(z\). It turns \(|0\rangle\) into the \(+\) superposition and is how you create superposition from a classical bit.

A quarter-turn phase flip: \(|0\rangle \to |0\rangle\), \(|1\rangle \to i|1\rangle\). \(S^2 = Z\). It is the discrete version of \(R_z\), and \(S^\dagger ZS = X\), so phase gates and X generate single-qubit Clifford operations.

QC::Qubits.f: How does a general single-qubit gate look?
QC::Qubits.b: Any one-qubit unitary is a rotation: \(U = e^{i\alpha}R_z(\gamma)R_y(\beta)R_z(\delta)\), with three parameters for \(2\times2\) unitaries modulo global phase. General rotations need a non-Clifford gate such as \(T = \mathrm{diag}(1, e^{i\pi/4})\).

QC::Qubits.f: What is the T gate and why does it matter?
QC::Qubits.b: \(T = \mathrm{diag}(1, e^{i\pi/4})\), a \(\pi/4\) phase. The Clifford group alone is not universal; adding \(T\) is, and \(T\) is not efficiently simulable classically. It is the source of essentially all the fault-tolerance cost.

QC::Qubits.f: What is a global phase, and why is it unphysical?
QC::Qubits.b: Multiplying \(|\psi\rangle\) by \(e^{i\theta}\) changes no probabilities, since \(|e^{i\theta}\alpha|^2 = |\alpha|^2\). So global phases are dropped, and two operators differing only by one act identically on states. Unitaries are equivalent up to this factor.

QC::Entanglement.b: Two or more qubits in a joint state that cannot be written as a product \(|\psi\rangle_{AB} = |a\rangle_A \otimes |b\rangle_B\). Measurement outcomes are correlated beyond anything classical local variables can reproduce.

\[ |\Phi^+\rangle = \frac{|00\rangle + |11\rangle}{\sqrt2}, \qquad |\Phi^-\rangle = \frac{|00\rangle - |11\rangle}{\sqrt2} \]
and the other pair, \(|\Psi^\pm\rangle = \frac{|01\rangle \pm |10\rangle}{\sqrt2}\). They are maximally entangled, with zero local information.

QC::Entanglement.f: How do you prepare a Bell pair in one step?
QC::Entanglement.b: Start from \(|00\rangle\), apply \(H\) to the first qubit, then \(\mathrm{CNOT}\) with the first as control: \(CNOT\cdot(H\otimes I)|00\rangle = |\Phi^+\rangle\). The pattern H then CNOT is the standard entangler.

QC::Entanglement.f: What correlation do Bell states show?
QC::Entanglement.b: Measuring in the same basis on both qubits gives perfectly identical outcomes for \(\Phi^\pm\) and perfectly opposite for \(\Psi^\pm\), always. No local hidden variable theory reproduces all four; that is Bell's theorem, tested to loophole-free standard.
If A and B are maximally entangled, A cannot be entangled with C at the same time. This is why entanglement is a resource, and it is the security argument behind quantum key distribution.

For a bipartite pure state, \(S_A = S_B = -\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_A \log \rho_A)\) and the total entropy is zero: you can measure A perfectly only by destroying A's link to B. For \(|\Phi^+\rangle\) the reduced state is \(\mathbb{1}/2\), so \(S = \ln 2\).

No. For unitary \(U\) and any unknown state, \(U(|0\rangle|0\rangle + |1\rangle|0\rangle)= U|0\rangle|0\rangle + U|1\rangle|0\rangle\) cannot equal \(|0\rangle|0\rangle + |1\rangle|1\rangle\), since the first summand forces \(U = I\). No-cloning holds even for imperfect copying (no-cloning with noise).

QC::Entanglement.f: Can you broadcast an unknown qubit to two receivers?
QC::Entanglement.b: No. Broadcasting requires cloning. The two no-go results differ in strength: no-cloning forbids copying regardless of entanglement, no-broadcast forbids distributing to several parties even if they start entangled.

QC::Entanglement.f: What is the controlled-Z gate used for?
QC::Entanglement.b: It applies \(Z\) to the target only if the control is 1, and it is symmetric in the two qubits. With Hadamards on both qubits it produces a phase kickback: \(\mathrm{CZ}(H\otimes H)|+\rangle|-\rangle = |-\rangle|-\rangle\). That converts a phase into a measurable bit, and is how \(Z\) and CNOT are built from \(H\) and CNOT.

Apply a gate to the target conditioned on a control, and the phase of the control state encodes information about the target. E.g. \(\mathrm{CNOT}\) sends \(|a\rangle|-\rangle \to |a\rangle|-a\rangle\). It is the standard trick for computing a function into the phase.

QC::Entanglement.f: Which two-qubit gates are CNOT and CZ, and are they related?
QC::Entanglement.b:
CNOT is a bit flip on the target, CZ a phase flip; both are symmetric under interchange. \[ \mathrm{CZ} = (I\otimes H)\,\mathrm{CNOT}\,(I\otimes H) \]
so any symmetric entangling gate gives both. CZ is the usual choice in trapped-ion and neutral-atom hardware; CNOT in superconducting and photonic.

QC::Entanglement.f: How do you get a Toffoli gate, and why do you care?
QC::Entanglement.b: \(\mathrm{CCX} = (I\otimes H)\,\mathrm{CNOT}\,(I\otimes H)\,\mathrm{CNOT}\). It is the universal classical gate: any reversible Boolean function is a composition of Toffoli and single-qubit gates, which is what makes quantum simulation of chemistry possible.

QC::Circuits.b: A network of gates acting on a register, read left to right or right to left depending on convention, ending in measurements. It is a compact description of a unitary followed by a measurement, and it is not reversible after measurement.

QC::Circuits.f: Why must quantum gates be unitary?
QC::Circuits.b: Unitarity gives \(\|\psi\|^2\) constant in time, i.e. conservation of total probability, and makes evolution reversible and norm-preserving. Non-unitary 'gates' (measurement, amplitude damping) are legitimate but stochastic and irreversible, which is exactly why they cannot be freely composed into a circuit.

The longest path through the circuit, in layers of parallel gates. It matters because decoherence grows with depth: the shallower the circuit, the more gates fit before errors accumulate. Optimising for depth, not gate count, is the right target.

QC::Circuits.f: What is the gate set {H, T, CNOT}?
QC::Circuits.b: A universal set: every unitary on n qubits can be built from it to arbitrary accuracy. Clifford gates \(\{H,S,CNOT\}\) are not universal but are cheap and simulable, and everything outside the Clifford group is expensive.

A block of gates reused many times. Without them, a linear-algebraic decomposition of a 1024-dimensional unitary has \(\sim 4^n\) parameters, so you would need exponentially many distinct gates; with a good ansatz (product states, low-depth layers) only polynomial.

QC::Circuits.f: Why is compiling to a hardware basis hard?
QC::Circuits.b: Because a single logical gate decomposes into many physical ones, and \(T\) and \(S\) have very different costs. Solovay-Kitaev gives \(O(\log^c(1/\varepsilon))\) overhead, but in practice phase-polynomial synthesis and the required *T-count* dominate.

Approximates any single-qubit gate to accuracy \(\varepsilon\) using a fixed finite gate set, with length \(O(\log^c(1/\varepsilon))\). Needed because hardware cannot implement arbitrary rotations exactly. The constants are still too large in practice, so the standard tool is phase-polynomial synthesis plus qubit-efficient routing.

QC::Circuits.f: What is transpilation, and what does it optimise?
QC::Circuits.b: Mapping a circuit onto a real device: choose the basis, route for connectivity, then optimise. The objective is \(2n\) SWAPs (or \(3n\) for a line) per long-range gate plus a big depth penalty, and the result is compared by expected cost, not gate count.

QC::Circuits.f: What is circuit cutting, and when is it used?
QC::Circuits.b: Partition a circuit so that each fragment is small enough to simulate classically, then reconstruct the expectation values from many fragment evaluations. The cost grows exponentially in the number of cuts, so it only pays for shallow circuits spread over many qubits -- the opposite regime from fault tolerance.

QC::Circuits.f: What is the difference between a gate model and an annealer?
QC::Circuits.b: A gate model is universal and exactly simulates quantum evolution, but needs error correction. An annealer (D-Wave) is a restricted Ising machine run adiabatically: far larger qubit counts, but it can only solve that one class of problem and is not universal.

QC::Algorithms.f: What is the quantum Fourier transform?
QC::Algorithms.b:
\[ \mathrm{QFT}|x\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{y=0}^{N-1} e^{2\pi i xy/N}|y\rangle \]
It is the quantum analogue of the FFT, and it maps phase information into the amplitudes, which is the reverse of what the classical FFT exploits.

QC::Algorithms.f: How many gates does the QFT need?
QC::Algorithms.b: \(O(n^2)\) for \(n\) qubits, because the Hadamards and controlled phase rotations at different distances cannot all run in parallel. It is cheap to apply but its output is scrambled, so reading it needs many measurements.

Shows a genuine quantum advantage on a promise problem: a function \(\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}\) known to be either constant or balanced. One query suffices versus \(2^{n-1}\) classically, via interference. It is the simplest witness that quantum computing changes asymptotics, though the problem is contrived.

QC::Algorithms.f: State Grover's algorithm and its cost.
QC::Algorithms.b: Searching \(N = 2^n\) unsorted items for a marked one takes \(O(\sqrt{N}) = 2^{n/2}\) queries with probability near 1, versus \(O(N)\) classically. The trick is amplitude amplification: about \((\pi/4)\sqrt{N}\) reflections about the mean and the marked state.

QC::Algorithms.f: What is the optimality caveat on Grover?
QC::Algorithms.b: The \(\sqrt{N}\) is optimal: BBBV proves any quantum search needs \(\Omega(\sqrt{N})\). It is a square-root, not exponential, speedup, so it only wins for enormous \(N\) -- and not against structured search problems that classical algorithms already handle in poly time.

QC::Algorithms.f: Why does Grover need multiple qubits?
QC::Algorithms.b: Diffusion is an \(n\)-qubit operation, so a search over \(2^n\) items needs an oracle acting on all \(n\) plus the extra ancilla for the phase oracle: about \(n+1\) qubits. Search for \(N\) items therefore needs \(\log_2 N + 1\) qubits, not \(N\).

QC::Algorithms.f: State Shor's factoring algorithm and its cost.
QC::Algorithms.b: Factors \(N\) in \(O((\log N)^3)\) time, versus the best classical sub-exponential (general number field sieve, roughly \(e^{O((\log N)^{1/3}(\log\log N)^{2/3})}\)). The exponential-in-input-size gap is the real result, not the \(O(n^3)\) itself.

QC::Algorithms.f: How does Shor's algorithm turn factoring into a period problem?
QC::Algorithms.b: Pick \(a\) coprime to \(N\), compute \(a^r \bmod N\). Fermat's little theorem says \(a^r = 1\) for some \(r\) dividing \(\varphi(N)\), so \(r\) is a period. QFT of \(|a^x \bmod N\rangle\) reveals \(r\) by finding peaks near \(kN'/r\), and \(\gcd\) gives a factor. The exponential speedup is in period finding.

QC::Algorithms.f: What is quantum simulation, and why is it expected to win first?
QC::Algorithms.b: Simulating another quantum system (chemistry, materials, lattice QCD) with a quantum computer. The output is a state that is generically exponential to describe, and the Hamiltonians are local and structured, so natural ansätze work. This needs no speedup argument at all: the problem itself is quantum.

QC::Algorithms.f: What is HHL, and why is it often dismissed?
QC::Algorithms.b: Linear-system solve in \(O(\log^2 N)\) given a good condition number and an efficient state-preparation/measurement oracle. The input preparation and readout are exponentially costly, so the honest end-to-end complexity is often worse than classical. It demonstrates a query-model speedup, not a practical one.

QC::Resources.f: What are the main quantum resource costs?
QC::Resources.b: Qubit count (memory, the hardest to scale), two-qubit gate count (the real time cost), T-count (the fault-tolerance cost), and depth (the decoherence budget). Optimising a circuit means trading these off, not minimising gate count.

QC::Resources.f: Why are T gates the expensive ones?
QC::Resources.b: Fault tolerance needs a code that can correct both bit and phase errors, which forces a large overhead. Within a surface code, each logical T gate costs roughly a few thousand physical gates, while Clifford gates are much cheaper. So T-count is the number that predicts hardware time, not the total gate count.

QC::Resources.f: What is qubit overhead in a fault-tolerant scheme?
QC::Resources.b: Roughly a factor \(d^2\) physical qubits per logical qubit, where \(d\) is the code distance. With \(d \sim 25\)-30 and thousands of logical qubits needed, that is millions of physical qubits, which is the main reason useful FTQC is out of reach today.

QC::Resources.f: What is a NISQ device and what limits it?
QC::Resources.b: Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum: tens to thousands of qubits with two-qubit error rates around \(10^{-3}\), far above the roughly \(10^{-10}\) an unprotected algorithm needs. No long computations are possible without error correction, so NISQ-era value is in demonstration and in error mitigation.

QC::Resources.f: What is zero-noise extrapolation, and what is its weakness?
QC::Resources.b: Run the circuit at several artificially amplified noise levels, fit the result against the noise parameter, and extrapolate back to zero. The weakness is that the extrapolation is a polynomial fit to a function that is not known to be polynomial, so it can be badly biased; it also costs a multiple of the circuit count.

Inserting idle periods of \(\pi\) pulses so that idle and gate noise partly cancel, extending \(T_2^*\) toward \(T_2\). It suppresses \(z\)-type error and a little \(xy\), but cannot remove gate errors, so it helps shallow circuits and not deep ones.

QC::Resources.f: What is readout error, and how is it handled?
QC::Resources.b: State-preparation and measurement error: the reported bit is wrong for a small fraction of shots. It is measured by preparing a known state many times, and mitigated by calibration matrices or by changing the assignment of outcomes. It is a calibration problem, not a coherence problem, so it is comparatively cheap to fix.

\(T_1\) is energy relaxation: the \(z\)-component of Bloch vector decays as \(e^{-t/T_1}\). \(T_2\) is dephasing, where the transverse component decays as \(e^{-t/T_2}\). Always \(T_2 \leq 2T_1\), and \(T_2^*\) is the even shorter observed dephasing from inhomogeneous broadening.

A hardware benchmark: the largest square circuit an average-width device can run so that the output distribution stays close to ideal. It counts qubits \(n\) and depth \(d\) as a single number \(2^d\), and it is a best-case metric, not a measure of useful performance.

QC::Resources.f: Which metric best predicts useful quantum advantage?
QC::Resources.b: Not qubits or volume, but logical operations before failure: how many error-corrected gates a device can sustain. A device with many noisy qubits is less useful than a small one with a small logical error rate, because advantage needs total error below a threshold across the whole computation.

QC::ErrorCorrection.f: Why is quantum error correction hard?
QC::ErrorCorrection.b: You cannot measure an error without collapsing the state, and you cannot copy the state to compare. The fix is redundancy in entangled subspaces, plus a rule that errors take a known, recoverable form. Knill-Laflamme: \(PEQ^\dagger P = c_{ab}E_a^\dagger E_b\).

QC::ErrorCorrection.f: What does the Knill-Laflamme condition say?
QC::ErrorCorrection.b: For a code correcting errors \(E_a\), it requires \(PEQ^\dagger P = c_{ab}E_a^\dagger E_b\). For a code that corrects an error exactly, \(P E_a^\dagger E_b P = c_{ab}P\): products of two errors act as scalars on the code space, so syndromes are computable without learning the logical state.

QC::ErrorCorrection.f: What is a syndrome, and why is measuring it safe?
QC::ErrorCorrection.b: Correlate the error with an auxiliary system and measure that. The logical state is untouched because the error operators act trivially on the code space: \(|\psi\rangle_L |0\rangle \to E_a|\psi\rangle_L|a\rangle\). You learn which error occurred without learning anything about the encoded amplitudes.

QC::ErrorCorrection.f: Does the 3-qubit bit-flip code correct phase errors?
QC::ErrorCorrection.b: No. It corrects a single \(X\) (bit flip) because \(|000\rangle\) and \(|111\rangle\) are the logical basis and both syndromes are distinct, but a single \(Z\) acts as a logical phase and is undetectable. You need at least three qubits to detect anything at all, since two errors are indistinguishable from one error plus a global phase.

QC::ErrorCorrection.f: How does the Shor 9-qubit code correct arbitrary single-qubit errors?
QC::ErrorCorrection.b: Concatenate three 3-qubit phase-flip codes, one per physical qubit, so a phase flip becomes a bit flip at the outer level, and correct that with the 3-qubit bit-flip code. Arbitrary errors decompose into \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) components, so this covers everything.

QC::ErrorCorrection.f: What does the threshold theorem say?
QC::ErrorCorrection.b: If physical error rates are below a threshold, arbitrarily long computations are possible with a polylogarithmic overhead in the ideal circuit size, by encoding with a growing code distance and concatenating. The threshold for surface codes is roughly \(10^{-2}\) to \(10^{-3}\) with good hardware and fast decoding.

A 2D topological code defined on a square lattice of qubits, with stabilizers \(A_v = X^{u_1}X^{u_2}X^{u_3}X^{u_4}\) on vertices and \(A_p = Z^{v_1}Z^{v_2}Z^{v_3}Z^{v_4}\) on faces, plus a global constraint. Its great virtue is locality: with only nearest-neighbour coupling you can still do universal computation via lattice surgery.

Merging and splitting logical qubits by stabiliser measurement instead of moving them physically. It avoids the extra ancilla and routing of code deformation, and the space cost is \(d\) rows of ancilla, which is why surface-code schedules are dominated by the \(d^2\) overhead.

Distil noisy \(|T\rangle\) states into cleaner ones by running a code on the encoded state, improving fidelity at the cost of more qubits and time. This is the standard way to reduce the T-count overhead, and it is what determines whether a fault-tolerant T gate is affordable.
